issues.title: THE BEAUTY OF AUTUMN
issues.subtitle: The Autumn Edit. From berry-stained lips and softly smoky eyes to the timeless glamour of red lipstick and the intimate ritual of getting ready, a celebration of beauty, nostalgia and the changing season.

articles.title: The Autumn Beauty Edit
articles.excerpt: The autumn 2026 beauty trends worth knowing, from berry lips and warm brown eyes to effortless, natural-looking skin.
articles.body:
The Autumn Beauty Edit

From berry-stained lips to softly smoky eyes, the beauty trends defining autumn 2026 and the timeless influences behind them.

There is something about the arrival of autumn that invites a little reinvention. As summer’s lighter colours give way to richer shades, our wardrobes begin to change, and naturally, so do our beauty routines. The lip gloss we reached for throughout July is replaced by something deeper, our everyday makeup becomes a little more defined, and suddenly, the idea of trying a new look feels particularly appealing.

For autumn 2026, beauty is finding a balance between nostalgia and modern simplicity. The influence of the 1990s remains unmistakable, but this season’s trends offer a softer, more wearable interpretation of the looks that once defined the supermodel era.

Perhaps the most noticeable return is the berry lip.

From sheer cherry stains to deep burgundy and wine-coloured lipstick, richer lip shades are becoming one of autumn’s defining beauty signatures. Unlike the heavily outlined, matte lips of previous decades, today’s interpretation often favours a softer finish. A berry tint gently blended into the lips can create an effortlessly polished look, particularly when paired with minimal eye makeup and fresh skin.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/october-beauty-2.jpg]]

For those who prefer something more understated, brown-toned makeup offers an equally timeless alternative.

Chocolate eyeshadow, softly smudged eyeliner and warm neutral shades have returned to the spotlight, recalling the beauty of 1990s icons such as Cindy Crawford and Kate Moss. The difference lies in the application. Rather than a dramatic smoky eye, autumn 2026 favours diffused colour, subtle definition and an almost effortless finish.

Even the complexion is becoming less complicated.

While luminous skin remains desirable, the emphasis has shifted towards allowing natural texture to show through. Lightweight coverage, carefully placed concealer and a touch of blush create a look that feels polished without appearing overly perfected.

The appeal of these trends lies partly in how easily they can become part of an everyday routine. A berry lip stain can transform the simplest outfit, while a little brown eyeliner offers an easy transition from daytime makeup to an evening look. Neither requires an entirely new collection of products, only a willingness to reinterpret what is already familiar.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/october-beauty-3.jpg]]

Beyond makeup, autumn’s beauty mood extends to the smallest details. Deep cherry manicures, glossy brunette hair and softly styled waves complement the season’s richer palette, creating an aesthetic that feels considered without becoming overly elaborate.

What makes autumn 2026 particularly interesting is its embrace of individuality. Rather than following one rigid beauty ideal, the season offers room for different interpretations, from barely-there makeup to a statement lip or more dramatic eyes.

Perhaps that is what makes the autumn beauty edit so appealing. It is not about changing everything with the arrival of a new season, but discovering how a few thoughtful details can make the familiar feel new again.

After all, sometimes a different shade of lipstick is all it takes.

articles.title: The Return of the Red Lip
articles.excerpt: From Marilyn Monroe to modern blurred berry lips, the enduring allure of a classic beauty statement.
articles.body:
The Return of the Red Lip

From the glamour of Old Hollywood to the blurred berry shades of 2026, the red lip is finding its place in a new generation’s beauty routine.

Few beauty statements have endured quite like the red lip. Across decades of changing trends, it has remained a symbol of confidence, femininity and effortless glamour. From the carefully painted lips of Hollywood actresses to the beauty looks dominating today’s runways, red lipstick has continually reinvented itself without ever losing its appeal.

During Hollywood’s golden age, actresses such as Marilyn Monroe and Elizabeth Taylor helped establish the red lip as an unmistakable signature of glamour. Paired with softly defined eyes and beautifully styled hair, it became an expression of elegance that would influence generations of women.

By the 1990s, the look had taken on a different character. Supermodels embraced deeper reds, brown-toned liners and richer textures, creating a mood that felt less polished and more individual. The red lip was no longer reserved for formal occasions. It could be worn with a simple black dress, a leather jacket or an otherwise understated outfit.

In 2026, the fascination continues, but the way we wear red lipstick is changing.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/october-lips-2.jpg]]

One of the year’s most recognisable beauty trends has been the blurred lip, popularised by celebrity makeup artist Nina Park. Rather than creating a perfectly defined outline, the technique involves softly blending colour towards the edges of the lips, producing a more natural, almost just-kissed appearance.

For autumn, this approach feels particularly relevant. Deep cherry, cranberry and wine shades offer a seasonal alternative to traditional bright red, while sheer stains and creamy textures make the look easier to incorporate into everyday makeup.

Yet the classic, precisely defined red lip is also enjoying renewed attention. At the September 2026 New York premiere of Verity, Dakota Johnson wore a striking cranberry-red lipstick with sharply defined edges, demonstrating that a more traditional approach can feel just as contemporary.

Perhaps the most appealing aspect of the red lip’s return is its versatility.

For daytime, a little berry lipstick pressed gently onto the lips and blended with a fingertip creates a softer finish. Paired with fresh skin, mascara and a simple hairstyle, the result feels elegant without appearing overly formal.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/october-lips-3.jpg]]

For an evening look, a deeper burgundy or classic crimson can become the centre of an otherwise minimal makeup routine. A matching lip liner offers definition, while a satin finish introduces a touch of sophistication without the intensity of a completely matte lipstick.

The key is finding an interpretation that feels personal. Some may prefer a sheer cherry tint, while others gravitate towards a bold red that becomes their signature. Neither requires an elaborate routine, and both can transform the simplest outfit.

What makes red lipstick so enduring is not merely its colour, but the feeling associated with wearing it. A familiar face in the mirror suddenly appears a little different, a little more considered, perhaps even a little more confident.

Decades after its most celebrated moments, the red lip remains one of beauty’s simplest forms of self-expression.

And perhaps that is why it never truly disappears. It simply waits for another generation to make it their own.

articles.title: The Ritual of Getting Ready
articles.excerpt: Fragrance, playlists, dressing tables and the pleasure of getting ready, whether for an evening out or simply for yourself.
articles.body:
The Ritual of Getting Ready

An ode to dressing tables, signature fragrances, favourite playlists and the quiet pleasure of turning an ordinary evening into an occasion.

There is a particular pleasure in getting ready for an evening out. The music playing in the background, a collection of makeup scattered across the dressing table, the familiar decision between two outfits that somehow takes longer than expected. Sometimes, the preparation becomes just as memorable as the evening itself.

In a world where everything seems to move increasingly quickly, the ritual of getting ready offers a rare opportunity to slow down. It is a moment devoted entirely to the little details, from choosing a favourite fragrance to fastening the final piece of jewellery.

Historically, the dressing table has represented more than a place to apply makeup. In eighteenth-century Europe, elaborate vanities became symbols of refinement, often adorned with mirrors, decorative boxes and delicate perfume bottles. They reflected a culture in which personal presentation was considered an art in itself.

Today, the ritual looks rather different. Beauty products sit beside phone chargers, playlists replace the quiet of traditional dressing rooms, and inspiration is often found through photographs saved on Pinterest or videos shared across social media.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/october-ritual-2.jpg]]

Yet the underlying fascination remains remarkably similar.

Perhaps one of the most personal elements of getting ready is fragrance. A signature perfume has the extraordinary ability to become associated with particular moments, people and places. The scent worn on a memorable evening can bring back its atmosphere long after the occasion has passed.

Then there is the makeup itself.

Some evenings call for a carefully defined lip and softly smoky eyes. Others require little more than mascara, a touch of blush and a favourite lip gloss. The beauty lies in the freedom to decide, experimenting with different looks without feeling obliged to follow every passing trend.

For autumn, this ritual takes on a particularly inviting atmosphere. Richer fragrances, berry-toned lips and softly styled hair complement the season’s darker evenings and more considered wardrobes. A favourite knit, a beautifully tailored coat or a simple black dress becomes part of the preparation.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/october-ritual-3.jpg]]

And perhaps the most enjoyable version of this ritual is the one shared with friends.

An evening spent getting ready together, borrowing a lipstick, exchanging opinions on outfits and laughing over a familiar playlist can become a memory in its own right. The photographs taken before leaving, the last-minute changes and the inevitable search for a missing earring are often as much a part of the occasion as the destination.

Of course, getting ready does not always require an elaborate plan. Sometimes, taking an extra few minutes to style one’s hair, put on a favourite fragrance or choose an outfit with care can make an ordinary day feel a little more special.

What makes these rituals meaningful is not the number of products used or the time spent in front of the mirror. It is the pleasure of doing something for oneself, without needing a particular reason.

Perhaps the true art of getting ready lies in understanding that beauty is not confined to the finished look.

Sometimes, the loveliest part of an evening happens before you even leave the house.

issues.title: THE RIVIERA ISSUE
issues.subtitle: La Dolce Vita. From the sun-drenched harbours of Portofino to the timeless glamour of Capri and Saint-Tropez, an exploration of Mediterranean elegance, vintage resort style and the art of living beautifully.

articles.title: The Art of the Italian Summer
articles.excerpt: Portofino, Capri and the enduring beauty of la dolce vita, where simple pleasures define an unforgettable season.
articles.body:
The Art of the Italian Summer

An exploration of the timeless allure of the Italian Riviera, where elegance, tradition and the art of living beautifully meet beneath the Mediterranean sun.

There is something about an Italian summer that seems to exist beyond the passing of time. Perhaps it is the warmth of the afternoon sun against pastel-coloured buildings, the sound of boats drifting through a harbour, or the quiet elegance of an aperitivo overlooking the Mediterranean. Whatever its secret, the Italian Riviera has long represented a particular vision of summer, one defined by beauty, simplicity and effortless sophistication.

Along the Ligurian coastline, Portofino has become synonymous with this ideal. Once a modest fishing village, its colourful waterfront gradually attracted an international circle of artists, actors and travellers. By the middle of the twentieth century, it had established itself as a fashionable retreat, celebrated for its picturesque harbour and unhurried atmosphere.

Further south, Capri offers another interpretation of Mediterranean glamour. With its dramatic cliffs, crystalline waters and celebrated Piazzetta, the island became a favourite destination of the international jet set during the 1950s and 1960s. Elegant women in silk scarves, oversized sunglasses and flowing summer dresses became part of a visual language that continues to define our imagination of the Italian summer.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/2mdB8CW00GSawB01KDRx74RFBfS65I9wVXEL6bhGrO1mHTl-EslRde6-MlJHCOwjrJ9yKUX6XNl-FI03JYc4ui_9gCE-pEa3Axh3cBrXM4MHsoXUpNwek1YNsRdG_w3yZh-JvaKPHybXfJKCgk9RtIVhpjNRCILdsb9XLw_Fwj5DCnSGnY944Pedm2VTtxnL.jpeg]]

At the heart of this fascination lies *la dolce vita*, the sweet life. Popularised internationally by Federico Fellini's 1960 film, the expression evokes a world of pleasure, beauty and sophistication. Yet beyond its glamorous associations, it reflects something more enduring: the Italian appreciation for everyday rituals.

A morning espresso at a neighbourhood café. A long lunch shared with family and friends. An evening spent watching the sun disappear beyond the coastline. These seemingly ordinary moments form the foundation of a lifestyle in which enjoyment is found in the simplest experiences.

Fashion has naturally played an essential role in shaping this image. The Riviera wardrobe favours beautifully cut linen, cotton dresses, woven sandals and silk scarves. Its elegance lies not in extravagance, but in an understated confidence that feels entirely at home beside the sea.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/pfi3Vv4xFGvxmYJCRFPDYmTvfa1ViuABDjYb7b5yT4830qcS-ZzCgv4TlHCVVprhI_hj2a7K6nxvmWht65VF2GR5krrJZLA9HQpawJyMPlVoSqzEiafFkQy5P4mq5pX6KUwqFYY0PMS7aZvhP_9AY4oqswSaJvsljlA4rXywFu2YLXP9V5tzUGx2gdUDx4xm.jpeg]]

Perhaps the most captivating element of the Italian summer, however, is its relationship with time. Afternoons unfold without urgency, meals become occasions, and the changing light across the water becomes something to appreciate rather than overlook.

Decades after the photographs of the 1950s and 1960s first captured the glamour of Mediterranean life, their atmosphere remains remarkably desirable. The Italian Riviera continues to inspire fashion, photography and travel, reminding us that certain ideals of beauty never truly disappear.

For the art of the Italian summer is not found in the grandest yacht or the most exclusive terrace. It exists in the quieter moments: the pleasure of good company, the elegance of simplicity and the ability to enjoy an afternoon without wishing it away.

The Italian summer has never been merely a season. It is a way of life.

articles.title: Slim Aarons: Photographing the Beautiful Life
articles.excerpt: The photographer who captured the glamorous world of the international jet set and shaped our vision of timeless luxury.
articles.body:
Slim Aarons: Photographing the Beautiful Life

The photographer who immortalised the glamour of the international jet set, capturing a world of sun-drenched terraces, elegant escapes and effortless sophistication.

Some photographs capture a moment. Others capture an entire way of life. For Slim Aarons, the distinction was almost inseparable.

Throughout the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, the American photographer became known for his extraordinary portraits of the international jet set. From the sunlit terraces of Capri to the glamorous swimming pools of the French Riviera, Aarons documented a world defined by leisure, elegance and an unmistakable sense of privilege.

Having worked as a combat photographer during the Second World War, Aarons later turned his attention towards a very different subject: the beautiful lives of society's most celebrated figures. His photographs offered a glimpse into private villas, exclusive resorts and Mediterranean retreats, revealing a world that appeared effortlessly removed from everyday life.

Yet what made his photography so distinctive was its apparent simplicity.

Rather than relying on elaborate studio settings, Aarons photographed his subjects within their own surroundings. A woman reclining beside a swimming pool, friends gathered beneath colourful parasols, or an elegant couple overlooking the coastline became scenes of extraordinary visual appeal.

His celebrated 1970 photograph Poolside Gossip, taken at the Kaufmann Desert House in Palm Springs, remains one of his most recognisable works. With its striking architecture, carefully balanced composition and casually glamorous subjects, the image embodies the atmosphere that made Aarons's photography so enduring.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/e482cd1Cj3Zit1ZVl0i30zSudIbniI2zxs4cUu70BWy1Btvs2JdH7nyOp0t2XxYr_7p98sltEx2IcmoFJm3Uqo5YVDxDcGCVKWU9j4CcoiAnlI0Njks9gmwZaGONrMzM4QJfUjj5cu61vFQUAXb803DoL56yRplIyQ9PqpmcWJU2uV_Fl8SyFBBxCKhfJ7qG.jpeg]]

The Mediterranean, however, provided some of his most captivating settings. In places such as Capri and the French Riviera, he captured an era when travel, fashion and social life became intertwined. His photographs transformed private moments of leisure into images that would shape the visual identity of luxury for generations.

There is a particular nostalgia within his work. The colours appear warmer, the afternoons longer, and the elegance almost instinctive. Yet behind this apparent spontaneity lies a remarkable understanding of composition, light and atmosphere.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/yARnB97cdEDSdh9GZFx56noOjIakGHnq1J-pyUzQjpTT0_uD_tvP5165kPIOgww7aQvdvlkIz2BXMvys49s5KdOLDJJr8A9tAl3xfpWHspQ-8-LV5bOQx0vwLVR5SdioJf2y7KeieCTGoJsj9WEXlSk8Ub9A8-qDrOkSJFgamSoc0Vdd8Z5-bN2TrZIiLRlW.jpeg]]

Today, his influence remains visible across fashion campaigns, luxury hospitality and contemporary editorial photography. The enduring fascination with vintage resort imagery, sun-drenched architecture and understated glamour owes much to the world he documented.

Perhaps the true beauty of Slim Aarons's photographs lies in their ability to make an ordinary afternoon feel extraordinary.

He did not simply photograph beautiful places. He captured the enduring fantasy of a beautiful life.

articles.title: The Riviera Wardrobe: An Enduring Elegance
articles.excerpt: From Bardot in Saint-Tropez to Jackie Kennedy in Capri, the silhouettes and accessories that made summer style timeless.
articles.body:
The Riviera Wardrobe: An Enduring Elegance

From Brigitte Bardot's effortless Saint-Tropez style to the timeless appeal of linen, silk scarves and sun-drenched sophistication.

There is a certain elegance that belongs exclusively to summer. It is less concerned with extravagance than with ease, less about following fashion than understanding the beauty of simplicity. Along the Mediterranean coastline, this philosophy of dressing has become an enduring expression of Riviera style.

During the 1950s and 1960s, the French and Italian Rivieras emerged as fashionable escapes for actors, artists and the international jet set. Their wardrobes reflected a new kind of sophistication, one that exchanged formal city dressing for relaxed silhouettes, lightweight fabrics and an unmistakable sense of freedom.

Few women embodied this transformation quite like Brigitte Bardot. In Saint-Tropez, her gingham dresses, ballet flats, wide-brimmed hats and effortlessly styled hair helped establish a new vision of summer femininity. Her appeal lay in the impression that elegance required little effort, even when every detail contributed to the look.

Across the Mediterranean, other style icons offered their own interpretations. Jackie Kennedy's summers in Capri introduced a polished approach to resort dressing, with tailored trousers, silk scarves and oversized sunglasses becoming defining elements of her wardrobe. Meanwhile, the relaxed glamour of Italian cinema brought flowing dresses, delicate sandals and beautifully understated accessories into the spotlight.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/r9_JdLWUn6wBlyuxmrWy61FTFjppAlF1VCJW6gaXaztQCYIRPqN4Rwc_jsJN2P0LvFHVQumOA_c3sm8XxklzRVcfpJRurCC_PWzlJrsftU0-RygGuLSTWR7cyu2P1xjHOYG9ZhOoeIPARVMI7vw3bcg3RqTWn3ToOi6pUrTSXrXX1UwXlKf0C6jbtCwyaxM8.jpeg]]

At the heart of Riviera fashion lies an appreciation for natural materials and timeless silhouettes. Crisp white cotton, softly structured linen and lightweight silk create a wardrobe designed to move effortlessly between afternoons by the sea and evenings overlooking the harbour.

Accessories provide the finishing touches. A silk scarf tied around the hair, woven basket bags, gold jewellery and oversized sunglasses transform the simplest ensemble into something memorable. Rather than competing for attention, each element contributes to a sense of quiet confidence.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/ZnMAofYEYkobADOE-wHzXHTm-vWAW_4-AtDiKX_BO-L09P4wB6EUGqdGy-pqhSy5Ak-igSUlMcpp5fEtgA54W1c7TtORiBNZXw6hYqoPCiSrWAXXifE3hf0zZ1P3wHvonrpyP93Se0kTUizSzhM3oVmgsX9Vnxf4eDISKcx1tYjIGFhUavsf87yFag-tEpra.jpeg]]

What makes this aesthetic particularly enduring is its resistance to passing trends. Decades after its most celebrated era, the Riviera wardrobe continues to inspire contemporary resort collections and summer editorials. The silhouettes may evolve, but the underlying philosophy remains remarkably consistent.

Perhaps this is the secret of Mediterranean style. Its beauty is not found in perfection, but in an attitude towards dressing that feels instinctive, personal and entirely unhurried.

For true Riviera elegance has never been about dressing for the occasion. It is about making simplicity unforgettable.

issues.title: THE JEWELLERY ISSUE
issues.subtitle: Objects of Desire. An exploration of the jewels that became icons, the extraordinary craftsmanship behind their creation, and the women whose stories made them unforgettable. From Cartier’s legendary Panthère to the enduring sentiment of heirlooms, this issue celebrates jewellery as art, memory and a timeless expression of individuality.

articles.title: The Cartier Panthère: An Icon of Timeless Luxury
articles.excerpt: The remarkable story of Cartier’s iconic panther, Jeanne Toussaint and the jewels that redefined daring elegance.
articles.body:
The Cartier Panthère: An Icon of Timeless Luxury

An enduring emblem of daring elegance, extraordinary craftsmanship and the women who made it legendary.

Certain symbols transcend the objects they adorn. They become a language of their own, instantly recognisable and endlessly reinterpreted. For Cartier, that symbol is the panther: poised, powerful and unmistakably elegant.

The feline first appeared in Cartier’s visual universe in 1914, when a wristwatch incorporated a pattern of diamonds and onyx recalling its spotted coat. That same year, an illustration by George Barbier featured a woman accompanied by a black panther. What began as a decorative motif would become one of the most distinctive signatures in jewellery history.

Its transformation into a legend is inseparable from Jeanne Toussaint. Appointed artistic director of Cartier’s high jewellery department in 1933, Toussaint brought an audacious spirit to the maison. Known for her exacting eye and instinctive sense of style, she saw in the panther a reflection of independence, strength and feminine confidence.

Under her direction, the animal moved beyond a pattern into fully realised sculptural jewels. The creatures appeared to crouch, climb and stretch across precious stones, their bodies articulated through intricate settings of diamonds, onyx and coloured gemstones.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/CN00034792.webp]]

One of the most celebrated examples was created in 1949 for the Duchess of Windsor: a diamond-and-sapphire panther poised above an extraordinary cabochon sapphire. The jewel was both extravagant and surprisingly alive, capturing the tension between wildness and refinement that defines the Panthère aesthetic.

The Duchess was among the great jewellery collectors of her time, and her remarkable Cartier pieces helped establish the panther as an emblem of fearless personal style. These were not ornaments intended to disappear into an outfit. They demanded attention, becoming part of the wearer’s identity.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/Cartier-Panther.jpg]]

That theatrical quality is balanced by the extraordinary precision of Cartier’s artisans. A panther’s expression may depend on the placement of two tiny emerald eyes; the suggestion of movement on the angle of a paw; its spotted coat on the delicate contrast between diamonds and dark stones. Each detail contributes to a creature that feels animated rather than merely decorative.

Across the decades, the panther has appeared in brooches, rings, bracelets and necklaces, sometimes rendered with extraordinary realism, sometimes reduced to an elegant silhouette. Whether resting against a vivid gemstone or curling around a wrist, the feline remains instantly recognisable.

Yet the lasting appeal of the Panthère is not simply its beauty. It represents a particular idea of luxury: one that embraces individuality, artistic risk and the confidence to wear something unforgettable.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/wilT6DJwqholwMECUL-gjtsV9QuqFVDRygP_veJ_t47eifNLyxV7YL53_XDP0uLswpm-UBYqgLw-M37sGet5Bgo1WPRxSrH1lq3IGQJ2wDwsYf2Xe_iw7eftnLz_96M2djLbL2rVVQu17SuhA2e_shkB7OVSjGIgulu7QFXLy2y8aZA2c367SDh9MtrlYOI2.jpeg]]

In a world where fashion continually searches for new symbols, Cartier’s panther needs no reinvention to remain relevant. Its power lies in its ability to move between eras without losing the character that made it iconic.

Some jewels are admired for their brilliance. Others become legends because they possess a spirit entirely their own.

articles.title: The Art of the Heirloom
articles.excerpt: From Van Cleef & Arpels to the memories carried across generations, an exploration of jewels that outlive their owners.
articles.body:
The Art of the Heirloom

Jewels That Outlive Generations

There is something profoundly intimate about a piece of jewellery that has lived more than one life. A necklace worn to a celebration decades ago, a ring passed from mother to daughter, or a bracelet whose significance lies not in its value, but in the memories it carries. Unlike so many objects we acquire, jewellery has the remarkable ability to remain with us, gathering meaning as the years pass.

Some pieces are treasured for their rarity, others for their craftsmanship. Yet the most extraordinary jewels often possess something less tangible: a history of their own.

Few jewellery houses capture this relationship between beauty, symbolism and sentiment quite like Van Cleef & Arpels.

Founded in Paris in 1906, the maison has long embraced a world of imagination, drawing inspiration from nature, romance and the delicate beauty of everyday life. Flowers, butterflies, fairies and celestial motifs have appeared throughout its collections, transforming precious materials into objects that seem to hold a story beyond their appearance.

Perhaps no creation expresses this philosophy more recognisably than the Alhambra.

Introduced in 1968, the collection began with a long necklace featuring twenty four-leaf clover-inspired motifs in textured yellow gold, each framed by a delicate border of golden beads. Its design was remarkably simple, yet immediately distinctive. Rather than relying upon the extravagance traditionally associated with high jewellery, the Alhambra offered an elegance that felt effortless, personal and entirely its own.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/francoisehardy-1-1024x802.jpg]]

The four-leaf clover had already occupied a special place in the history of the maison. Jacques Arpels, nephew of the founding couple, was known for collecting clovers and offering them as tokens of good fortune. For him, luck was not merely a symbol, but something to be believed in and shared.

This sentiment became central to the Alhambra’s identity. A necklace was no longer simply an ornament; it could become a personal talisman, a quiet reminder of hope, affection or a meaningful moment.

Throughout the 1970s, the collection found admirers among women celebrated for their elegance, including Grace Kelly, Princess of Monaco, and French actress Romy Schneider. Worn with eveningwear or more relaxed silhouettes, its delicate motifs reflected a changing approach to luxury, one in which precious jewellery could become part of everyday personal style.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/0bc70269a0a43dcaed143b06d008a023.jpg]]

Over the decades, the Alhambra has evolved through different materials and interpretations. Mother-of-pearl lends the design a soft luminosity, while onyx introduces a striking contrast. Malachite, carnelian and variations in gold offer entirely different expressions of the same familiar silhouette.

Yet what makes the collection particularly fascinating is the consistency of its design. Despite changing fashions, the four-leaf motif remains unmistakable. Its proportions, rounded edges and delicate beaded frame have become a visual signature that connects contemporary creations with the original design.

Behind this apparent simplicity lies a tradition of meticulous craftsmanship.

The beauty of fine jewellery is often found in details that are barely noticed at first glance. The careful selection of stones, the precision of polishing and the delicate construction of each setting require an extraordinary degree of patience. At Van Cleef & Arpels, this dedication to artistry has long formed part of the house’s identity.

Its celebrated Mystery Set technique, patented in 1933, offers another expression of this expertise. Through an intricate method of securing carefully cut gemstones onto concealed metal rails, the maison’s artisans create surfaces in which precious stones appear almost uninterrupted by their settings. The result is a remarkable illusion of colour, texture and light.

[[image:https://isabellata.github.io/maison-verve/iMPupAVpTF83pe4kfN9Jhi-1920-80.jpg.webp]]

Although distinct from the Alhambra collection, this innovation reflects the same commitment to craftsmanship that allows jewellery to retain its beauty across generations.

And perhaps this is where the true meaning of an heirloom begins.

A piece of jewellery does not become significant simply because it is expensive, nor does age alone make it precious. Its meaning develops through the people who wear it, the occasions it accompanies and the memories gradually attached to it.

A pendant received on a birthday may one day become a daughter’s most treasured possession. A bracelet worn throughout someone’s life might eventually tell a story that photographs and letters cannot fully capture. The object remains unchanged, yet its significance becomes richer with every generation.

In this way, jewellery occupies a unique place between fashion and memory. Clothing may reflect a particular moment, and trends inevitably evolve, but certain jewels move quietly through time, adapting to new lives without losing their original sentiment.

The enduring appeal of Van Cleef & Arpels lies partly in this ability to create pieces that feel both recognisable and deeply personal. The Alhambra may be celebrated throughout the world, but the meaning attached to an individual necklace or bracelet belongs entirely to its wearer.

Perhaps the most beautiful jewels are not those that attract the greatest attention, but those that become inseparable from the people who own them.

For while gold may preserve its brilliance and gemstones their colour, it is memory that gives an heirloom its most enduring value.

Some jewels are made to be worn. Others are destined to be remembered.

articles.title: Diamonds, Icons & the Women Who Wore Them
articles.excerpt: Elizabeth Taylor, Grace Kelly and Princess Diana: the women who transformed extraordinary jewels into enduring legends.
articles.body:
Diamonds, Icons & the Women Who Wore Them

An exploration of the extraordinary jewels and unforgettable women who transformed diamonds into symbols of glamour, individuality and enduring elegance.

There are jewels that are remembered for their extraordinary beauty, and others that become inseparable from the women who wore them. A diamond necklace photographed beneath the lights of Hollywood, a sapphire ring worn by a princess, or an emerald that once belonged to a celebrated actress. Beyond their brilliance, these pieces carry something far more captivating: the stories of the women who made them unforgettable.

Throughout history, jewellery has represented wealth, status and refinement. Yet in the hands of certain women, precious stones became something more personal. They reflected individuality, confidence and a particular understanding of elegance that could never be defined by fashion alone.

Few women understood the extraordinary allure of jewellery quite like Elizabeth Taylor.

With her violet eyes, dark hair and unmistakable Hollywood presence, Taylor embodied a kind of glamour that belonged entirely to another era. Her appreciation for fine jewellery was legendary, and over the course of her life she assembled one of the most remarkable private collections of precious stones in the world.

Among her most celebrated possessions was the 33.19-carat Krupp Diamond, gifted to her by Richard Burton in 1968. Its remarkable size and clarity made it extraordinary, but it was Taylor’s affection for the stone that gave it a personality of its own. She wore it with evening gowns, elaborate hairstyles and the confidence of a woman who considered magnificent jewellery something to be enjoyed rather than hidden away.

Another unforgettable treasure was the historic La Peregrina pearl, also presented to her by Burton. Once associated with European royalty, the pearl was eventually incorporated into an elaborate necklace designed by Cartier, surrounded by diamonds, rubies and pearls.

Taylor’s collection reflected a fascination not simply with extravagance, but with the history and romance of beautiful objects. For her, jewels were never merely accessories. They were treasured companions, each connected to a particular moment, relationship or memory.

If Elizabeth Taylor represented the theatrical splendour of Hollywood, Grace Kelly offered a quieter interpretation of luxury.

Before becoming Princess of Monaco, Kelly had already established herself as one of cinema’s most elegant figures. Her understated beauty, immaculate tailoring and graceful presence made her a symbol of mid-century sophistication. When she married Prince Rainier III in 1956, her personal style entered a new chapter, one defined by the traditions and splendour of royal life.

Her engagement ring, created by Cartier, featured an emerald-cut diamond weighing approximately 10.47 carats, flanked by two baguette diamonds. Remarkably refined despite its extraordinary size, the ring reflected the balance between grandeur and simplicity that came to define Kelly’s image.

Throughout her years as Princess of Monaco, she wore magnificent jewellery with an elegance that rarely appeared excessive. Diamond tiaras, pearl necklaces and precious stones complemented her wardrobe, yet never seemed to overpower the woman wearing them.

Her enduring influence lies partly in this restraint. Where others embraced extravagance, Kelly demonstrated that the most powerful expression of luxury could be remarkably subtle.

Decades later, Diana, Princess of Wales, would introduce a different kind of royal jewellery iconography.

Diana’s jewellery became an extension of her evolving public identity. From the romantic elegance of her early royal appearances to the increasingly confident style of her later years, her choices reflected a woman developing a visual language of her own.

Perhaps no piece is more closely associated with her than her sapphire engagement ring, selected in 1981. Created by Garrard, the ring features a large oval blue sapphire surrounded by fourteen solitaire diamonds. Its striking colour and distinctive design made it instantly recognisable, setting it apart from more conventional diamond engagement rings.

Yet Diana’s influence extended beyond a single piece.

She frequently reimagined the way royal jewellery could be worn, pairing traditional pieces with contemporary eveningwear and occasionally transforming necklaces into unexpected accessories. One particularly memorable appearance came in 1985, when she wore an emerald-and-diamond choker as a headband during a visit to Australia.

It was a small act of individuality, but one that captured her ability to reinterpret tradition without abandoning it.

Unlike the carefully controlled formality often associated with royal jewellery, Diana’s approach felt expressive, modern and deeply personal. Her jewels were beautiful, but the way she wore them made them memorable.

What connects these three women is not simply their access to extraordinary collections. It is their ability to give precious objects an identity beyond their material value.

Elizabeth Taylor brought diamonds into a world of romance and cinematic extravagance. Grace Kelly transformed magnificent jewels into expressions of composure and timeless refinement. Princess Diana challenged convention, introducing a more personal and contemporary understanding of royal elegance.

Their jewellery continues to fascinate because it offers a glimpse into lives that have become part of cultural history. Photographs preserve the brilliance of the stones, but also the gestures, expressions and moments that made them significant.

In an age where luxury is often associated with novelty, these archival images remind us that true elegance is rarely confined to a particular decade. The most memorable jewels do not lose their beauty when fashions change. Instead, they acquire new meaning through the women who wore them.

Perhaps diamonds have always been admired for their ability to endure. Yet their most extraordinary quality may be the memories they preserve.

For a jewel may possess remarkable beauty, but it is the woman who wears it who makes it unforgettable.
